question.leadin: In trying to escape from the capital of this empire, Spanish soldiers experienced La Noche Triste [la no-chay tree-stay].
question.text: Name this empire, led by Montezuma, which was conquered by Hernan Cortes in 1521.
question.clue: Its last ruler was Cuitlahuac, the younger brother of Montezuma II.

swap.text: The Aztecs, meanwhile, used this language, whose modern variety is still widely spoken today. The words "chipotle" and "axolotl" come from this language.
swap.clue: Historians learned to write in this language at schools called calmecacs ("kahl-MAY-kahks").

question.leadin: Answer these questions about the native peoples of the Americas.
question.text: Sites from this Mesoamerican civilization include La Venta and San Lorenzo, which were mysteriously abandoned. They created giant stone heads, thought to be depictions of their rulers.
question.clue: This culture created "elongated man" figurines as well as a greenstone statue of a man holding a were-jaguar ("wair-jaguar").

swap.leadin: Answer the following about Mesoamerican civilizations based in Mexico.
swap.text: These people built a great step pyramid in their city of Chichen Itza. This civilization had a Long Count calendar that some believed suggested that the end of the world would occur in 2012.
swap.clue: King Pacal of these people was born on 9.8.9.13.0 in this people's "Long Count" calendar.

question.text: The Colossal Heads were created by this earliest major civilization of Mesoamerica, who were the first to play the mesoamerican ballgame. This culture's writing system may have influenced the later Mayan hieroglyphics system.
question.clue: Much of their art is based on a jaguar god, including much in that capital, La Venta.

swap.leadin: The Dresden and Madrid codices contain this culture's writing, and their cities include Palenque (puh-LEN-kay) and Yaxchilan (YAA-shee-lan).
swap.text: Name this civilization, whose Long Count calendar allowed it to mark dates longer than the 52-year "round" used by its 260 and 365-day calendars.
swap.clue: The Temple of Inscriptions houses anajaw("ah-how")from this civilizationknown as Pacal the Great who reigned for 68 years in its city-state of Palenque("pah-LEN-kay").

question.text: Inscriptions in this city lead by Pakal the Great indicate it went into a star war with another in 672 CE. An overgrown jungle in Chiapas now partly covers this city where the ball game was probably played near the Temple of the Inscriptions.
question.clue: The French explorer Jean-Frederic Waldeck resided for a time at this city, where a leafy corn plant mural is located at its "foliated cross" complex.

swap.text: Under the presidency of Efrain Rios Montt, the Guatemalan government committed a genocide against these peoples, killing almost 40% of them. One of these people won the 1992 Nobel Peace Prize for her autobiography.
swap.answerHtml: Maya peoples [accept K’iche’; accept Q’eqchi’] (The autobiography is I, Rigoberta Menchú.)
swap.clue: The modern-day Zapatista Army of National Liberation in Chiapas, inspired by Zapata's agrarian reforms, is majority-run by these peoples. Also in Chiapas is this ethnic group's city of Palenque.

question.leadin: Alfonso Caso established a chronology for this site consisting of five periods, and discovered its extensive "Tomb Seven" shrine.
question.text: Name this archaeological site. Hundreds of artistic figures found here termed "Danzantes" suggest that the inhabiting civilization practiced human sacrifice.
question.clue: Another monument depicts men with scrolls in place of their genitalia who likely represent mutilated war captives - that being the Temple of the Danzantes, or the "Building of the Dancers."

swap.text: Large numbers of children from this ethnic group were abducted after massacres carried out by forces loyal to Efrain Rios Montt in Guatemala. Rigoberta Menchu, a member of this indigenous group, won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1992.
swap.answerHtml: Maya [accept K'iche' Maya; prompt on indigenous peoples or Native Americans or Indians]
swap.clue: A revolt of these people began a fifty-year long Caste War in the second half of the 19th century.

question.leadin: Civilizations utilizing this system also used a smaller-scale system with Haab' and Tzolk'in components.
question.text: Identify this primarily base-20 system. The end of a b'ak'tun was predicted by this system's Long Count.
question.clue: The Book of Chilam Balam of Chumayel discusses this system, which was split into the divine Tzolk'in and civil Haab' derived from "Venus rounds."

swap.leadin: Identify these pre-Columbian civilizations of the Americas.
swap.text: This civilization founded a number of city-states in the Yucutan Peninsula, including Tikal and Chichen Itza.
swap.clue: Pakal was one ruler of this civilization, which used cenotes (suh-no-tays) for the worship of their rain god.

question.text: This conquistador contracted the scholar Francisco Lopez de Gomara to write an account of his conquest of Tenochtitlan ("teh-nohch-teet-LAHN").
question.answerHtml: Hernán Cortés [or Hernán Cortés de Monroy y Pizarro Altamirano]
question.clue: The Florentine Codex details how this man's subordinate, Pedro de Alvarado, massacred most of the people at a festival in the Templo Mayor, leading to the retaliatory murder of this man's soldiers during La Noche Triste.

swap.leadin: This city's emblem glyph is the most widely distributed of all such glyphs in the Americas.
swap.text: Name this city whose ruler Sky Witness achieved a major power reversal by converting Caracol from a vassal of this city's rival Tikal into an ally. Today, this city is identified as the capital of the "Kingdom of the Snake."
swap.clue: This Snake Kingdom known for being the bitter enemy of Tikal during the Classical Mayan period.

question.leadin: Alfred V. Kidder identified Verapaz as a site of trade between these two broad areas, which included a zone that was dominated by the early hydraulic state of Kaminaljuyu ("ka-mee-nal-HOO-yoo") during the Late Preclassic period.
question.text: Give these two geographic terms that delimit the two centers of Maya civilization. One of these two zones is divided into a northern area that includes Coba and Izamal and southern sites like Seibal and Uaxactun ("wah-shahk-TOON") in Peten.
question.answerHtml: Highlands AND Lowlands [accept área meridional in place of “Highlands”; accept Northern Lowlands, área septentrional, Southern Lowlands, or área central in place of “Lowlands”]

swap.text: The two classes of elite Aztec warriors that used the macuahuitl and recruited from all social classes were named after eagles and these animals.
swap.answerHtml: jaguars [or ocēlōtl; accept jaguar warriors; accept jaguar knights; prompt on cats]
swap.clue: Strange stone statues with cleft heads, such as many found by Matthew Stirling, represent an art motif referred to as a "were- ."

question.text: This ceremonial center of the Mayan civilization is located in modern-day Guatemala, and features a notable Temple of the Jaguar.
question.clue: This polity's rival was called the Snake Kingdom, and this polity's namesake hiatus began after its ruler Wak Chan K'awiil was defeated by this polity's rival and Caracol.

swap.text: The Tarascans battled this eighth king of the Aztecs, who was succeeded by Moctezuma II in 1502. This fellow famously built a temple of skulls from the sacrifced victims of the Flower Wars, and took his name from a legendary water monster.
swap.clue: Advised by his uncle Tlacaellel, this man dedicated the Templo Mayor, and gained infamy for his massive displays of human sacrifice.

question.text: The Sun Dagger glyph at this 'observatory' in New Mexico marked the position of the Sun during solstices and equinoxes. This 'observatory' containing the Fajada Butte was an important ritual site for the Pueblo people who lived in "great houses" at this 'observatory'.
question.clue: Near this site, Anna Sofaer documented a spiral petroglyph called the Sun Dagger that may track an 18.6-year lunar cycle.

swap.text: This civilization sacked the Mayan city of Teotihuacan. They had their capital at Tula, Hidalgo and faced the nomadic Chichimec people.
swap.clue: It's not Teotihuacan, but the Mexica ("may-SHE"-kah) passed through the ruins of this culture's capital on their way to settling the Valley of Mexico, which inspired the layout of Tenochtitlan and other Aztec cities.
